solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Dodgy dealer important people returned to see

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: VIPs are very important people

explanation.surface: A shady trader whom the bigwigs come back to visit.
explanation.walkthrough: A spiv is British slang for a flashy small-time crook who deals in black-market goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiv makes a living through shady trading, so he is literally a dodgy dealer in British usage.

clue.text: Fellow in a hat's unsettled girl

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is placed within the other
something unsettled is disturbed from its order, so these letters get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the possessive S included
a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A man wearing a hat makes a young woman uneasy.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's counts as a letter of the scrambled material, and the fellow is slotted into the middle of the rearranged result.
explanation.definitionFit: Samantha is a common female first name, so it is one example of a girl's name.

clue.text: Tongue and part of eye itch at the bottom

parts.note: the iris is the coloured part of the eye

indicators.note: in a down entry the bottom of a word is its final letter, so only the end is kept

parts.note: the last letter of itch

explanation.surface: An itchy tongue and eye, reading like a list of ailments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' looks like the body part beside the eye, but it means a language.
explanation.definitionFit: Tongue is an old word for a language, and Irish is the Celtic language spoken in Ireland.

clue.text: After panic, lift biscuit

indicators.note: coming after something places it second, which sets the order the parts join in

parts.note: a flap is a state of panic, as in 'in a flap'
to jack is to lift, as with a car jack

explanation.surface: Once the panic subsides, someone grabs a biscuit for comfort.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a flapjack is a chewy oat bar made with butter and syrup, not a pancake as in America.
explanation.definitionFit: British flapjacks are baked oat slices sold beside cookies, loosely classed with biscuits in shops and tins.

clue.text: Nightingale, having disturbed maple, had to fly

indicators.note: things disturbed are knocked out of place, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A songbird, startled out of a maple tree, takes off.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a bird, but the capital N points to Florence Nightingale, the nurse of the Crimean War.
explanation.definitionFit: Florence Nightingale earned the nickname from her night rounds among wounded soldiers carrying a lantern.

clue.text: Devotion of shepherd's maybe timely in the extreme

parts.note: shepherd's pie is one kind of pie, so 'maybe' marks an example

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of timely

explanation.surface: A shepherd's dedication to his flock, extremely well timed.
explanation.walkthrough: Shepherd's pie is minced lamb topped with mashed potato; here 'shepherd's' needs the word pie supplied.
explanation.definitionFit: Piety is religious reverence, the quality of being devout, which is close to devotion as a noun.

clue.text: Disreputable person you wouldn't want at breakfast!

definitions.text: Disreputable person you wouldn't want at breakfast!

parts.note: the surface reading: a person of poor character
the setter's reading: a rotten item served on the breakfast plate

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for a rogue is taken literally as a rotten item from the hen house that would spoil a fry-up.
explanation.definitionFit: An old idiom calls a dishonest or untrustworthy person a rotten one of these, exactly as the breakfast joke suggests.

clue.text: Tackle header or footer on elaborate flyer

parts.note: kit is gear or equipment, as is tackle

indicators.note: a word's header and footer are its first and last letters, and here either one serves

parts.note: elaborate begins and ends with the same letter

explanation.surface: Taking on a fancy aircraft from top to bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: Elaborate starts and ends with E, so 'header or footer' gives the same letter either way.
explanation.definitionFit: A kite is a toy that flies on a string, and it is also a bird of prey, either way a flying thing.

clue.text: Something shiny and small, associated with horses mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
equine means relating to horses; its last letter is cut

explanation.surface: A small sparkly decoration on a show horse's harness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Associated with horses' is a single adjective, not a phrase about stables; 'mostly' trims its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A sequin is a small glittering disc sewn onto clothing, an ornament whose whole purpose is to catch light.

clue.text: Girl (2, possibly) Mother and I study

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
taken as written
to read a subject is to study it at university

explanation.surface: A girl tells us that she and her mother are studying.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 2 points to 2 down, IRISH: the girl's name is one typically Irish.
explanation.definitionFit: Mairead is the Irish Gaelic form of Margaret, so it is an example of a girl's name from Ireland.

clue.text: Old part of play is spot on

parts.note: ex- means former, as in ex-wife
a play is divided into acts

explanation.surface: A section of an old drama is judged perfectly done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' is the prefix for former things, as in ex-husband, rather than an adjective about the play.
explanation.definitionFit: Spot on is a British idiom for completely accurate or correct, the same sense as precise.

clue.text: Indian statesman turned heads in unison, recalling his entourage noisily

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so the letters read backwards
the head of a word is its leading letter, so only the starts are taken

parts.note: the opening letters of these five words

explanation.surface: A statesman's followers all turn their heads together as he loudly summons them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' only links: the leading letters come from the five words that follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: Jawaharlal Nehru was the first Prime Minister of independent India, a leading political figure there.

clue.text: O for a breather!

parts.note: the surface reading: a sigh of longing for a rest
the setter's reading: O is the chemical symbol of the gas that anyone breathing needs

explanation.walkthrough: 'O for' is the poetic cry of longing, as in 'O for a muse of fire'; read literally, O stands for a chemical element.
explanation.definitionFit: The element with symbol O is the gas every breathing creature draws in, so a breather needs it.

clue.text: Turns to remove international body's teams

parts.note: the UN is the United Nations, with the possessive S
crews are teams working together

explanation.surface: Rotating the United Nations' squads out of their posts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns to remove' looks like a verb about rotation of staff, but it describes twisting a screw out.
explanation.definitionFit: To unscrew a lid or bolt is to twist it round until it comes off, which is rotating it to detach it.

clue.text: Be uninformed about what nudists do?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to hold no information on a subject or person
second meaning: to wear no clothes at all

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second meaning, taking the idiom about knowledge literally as being unclothed.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both lacking any evidence or knowledge about something and wearing no clothing whatsoever.

clue.text: Discover me erotically hugging old artist

indicators.note: to hug is to hold something closely inside, so the words grip a run of letters

parts.note: a run of letters across the three words

explanation.surface: An invitation to romance, someone embracing a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across discoVER ME ERotically.
explanation.definitionFit: Johannes Vermeer was a seventeenth-century Dutch painter, famous for Girl with a Pearl Earring.

clue.text: Middle Easterners of enormous IQ, aristocratic, turning up

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up sends letters back toward the top, so they read backwards
of here means taken out of, so a string comes from within the words

parts.note: a run of letters across the three words

explanation.surface: Brainy, high-born people from the Middle East showing up.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is enormouS IQ ARIstocratic, which reads backwards in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Iraqis are the people of Iraq, a country in the Middle East, so they are Middle Easterners.

clue.text: French cheeses, we hear, or piece of cake?

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken, so the answer matches a sound rather than a spelling

parts.note: Brie is a soft French cheese

explanation.surface: A dessert choice: a plate of French cheeses or a slice of gâteau.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of cake' looks like a food on the menu, but it is the idiom for something easy.
explanation.definitionFit: A breeze and a piece of cake are both informal idioms for a task that is very easy.

clue.text: Venue's not opening without first bit of something to follow

indicators.note: without its opening means the leading letter is lost
without in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: venue loses its first letter; the 's reads as possessive

indicators.note: the first bit of a word is just its initial letter

parts.note: the opening letter of something

explanation.surface: A venue that won't open until something else comes after.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking', but here it carries its old meaning of outside.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to happen afterwards as a result, which is to come after or succeed something.

clue.text: Old Mexican detective following two in centre of piazza

indicators.note: one thing following another comes after it, which fixes the order
two at the centre means the middle pair of letters

parts.note: the middle two letters of piazza
tec is short for detective

explanation.surface: An elderly Mexican sleuth tails two people across the middle of a town square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detective' is not the definition; tec is the crossword's standard short form for a sleuth, placed after the pair from piazza.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aztecs were the people who ruled central Mexico before the Spanish conquest of the sixteenth century.

clue.text: Find tiny amount

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to track down or locate
second meaning: a very small quantity

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an instruction to find a little of something; the verb and the noun are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to track down by following clues; as a noun it means the barest detectable quantity.

clue.text: Bark with ring, soft in the middle

parts.note: W is an abbreviation for with
a ring is round like the letter O

indicators.note: the middle of a word is what is left between its ends, so only the inner letters stay

parts.note: the inner two letters of soft

explanation.surface: A tree's bark with a ring in it, gone soft in the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soft' tempts as P, the musical abbreviation, but here the inner letters of the word are wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Woof is the sound a dog makes, so it is a bark in the canine sense, as a noun or verb.

clue.text: At front of Gents, old signs

indicators.note: placed at the front means set before the rest, which fixes the order

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
the gents and the men's are both names for a men's toilet

explanation.surface: Old signs hanging at the entrance to the gents' toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'the Gents' is a public men's toilet, also signed 'Men's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Omens are portents or signs of what is to come, foretelling good or bad fortune.

clue.text: A private (US) art gallery displays rock

parts.note: taken as written
a GI is an American private soldier
the Tate is a group of London art galleries

explanation.surface: An American soldier's gallery shows off a geological exhibit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' looks like a noun on display, but it is the verb meaning to shake.
explanation.definitionFit: To rock something is to shake or disturb it, which is what agitate means as a verb.

clue.text: Ref spoke in a frenzy, always

indicators.note: a frenzy is wild disorder, so these letters are thrown about

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A referee who is always ranting wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoke' looks like the verb of the ref's outburst, but its letters join REF as raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Something kept for keeps is held permanently, an idiom for forever or for good.

clue.text: Jokiness — not OK in a girl

indicators.note: saying not means leaving out, so the named letters are removed

parts.note: taken as written
the letters to strike out, taken literally

explanation.surface: A girl whose humour is not quite all right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as a link to the girl, but it is part of what is taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: Jess is a familiar female first name, short for Jessica, so it is one example of a girl.
